name: Ben Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for agreeing to talk. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights mostly, covering the docks and the industrial estate on the north bank, plus the pubs along Quay Street. It's quiet for an hour and then three things at once: an alarm at a warehouse, a lorry driver asleep at the wheel in a lay-by, a fight at closing time. I like nights because you get proper jobs and fewer meetings. My dad was a firefighter for thirty years, so I grew up thinking a uniform job is a proper job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the team, and I like that the dock workers know me and will flag me down. Tough is sleep, and the feeling that the city spends money on gadgets instead of officers. I use AI now and then, mostly when the lads on my shift show me something that actually works. Saturdays I help drive the church food bank van, and I do woodwork in my dad's garage when I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad would say: a lot of noise about nothing. At work I'd tell the lads to stop worrying and get on with it. I'm not on social media much, so that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. The job's steady, the pay covers rent and a bit of saving, and Hanna and I can keep planning. I've got about three months of savings, and the main pressure is just getting a house deposit together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. Keep putting 250 a month away for the deposit. If a tool comes in that the other lads swear by, I'd try it, and if not, I'd leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a storm warning that turned out to be drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Hanna. What does she do, and does any of this touch her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hanna's a nurse at a care home on the edge of town. Nothing in this picture touches her job, if anything they need more people. The only thing that worries us is the price of houses, same as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the city spends on gadgets instead of officers. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year they bought number-plate cameras for the whole ring road and then cut two posts on my team. The cameras are fine, but a camera doesn't sit with a drunk lad until the lad's mum comes to collect him. I'd want the money spent on people.

say: I'd say it was a lot of **noise** about nothing, like my dad would.
I'd tell the lads to **stop worrying** and get on with it.
think: I'm **glad**: the job's steady and the pay covers rent and saving.
The main pressure is still a **house deposit**.
do: Keep saving **250 a month** for a deposit.
Try a tool only if **the other lads** swear by it.
feel: **Calm**, like a storm warning that turned out to be **drizzle**.
S0.quote: A camera doesn't sit with a drunk lad until the lad's mum comes to collect him.
fieldNote: His view of work comes from his **firefighter father**.
He's annoyed by **spending on gadgets** over officers, a long-held gripe.
His partner's **care home job** feels solid to him in every picture.

steps.text: Keep working nights on the docks and Quay Street
Keep saving 250 a month towards a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any big change, the ones who put the work in come out fine. At work I'd tell the lads to learn the new kit properly instead of moaning. I'd say the force should get proven systems, not whatever's newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the control room and the back office get hit, and I'd feel for them. Out on the docks I'd still be doing most of the same things. What I'd worry about is the bosses using the time saved as an excuse to cut more officers, like they did with the cameras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a couple of months until the systems settle, then learn them properly, maybe sit the course in the first six months. I'd keep saving the 250. I wouldn't change anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not for myself so much. More for the people indoors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who indoors would you be thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen in the control room, who's been dispatching us for twenty-odd years. If software starts deciding which car goes where, Maureen (a dispatcher at his station) would be the first to go. She knows the docks better than any map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell the lads to stop moaning. Would you moan yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, in the van. Everyone does. But I'd still turn up for the training, because that's the job.

say: I'd say people who **put the work in** come out fine.
I'd say the force should buy **proven systems**, not the newest.
think: The **control room** and back office get hit, not the docks patrol.
Bosses might use saved time as an excuse to **cut officers**.
do: Learn the **new systems** properly within six months.
Keep saving **250 a month** and change nothing big.
Wait a couple of months for the systems to **settle** before starting.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for **people indoors** than for himself.
S1.quote: If software starts deciding which car goes where, Maureen (a dispatcher at his station) would be the first to go.
fieldNote: He backs **hard work** as the answer but worries about **cuts** from above.
He thinks of an **older dispatcher** first.
He'd moan **in the van** but still turn up, a steady man's habit.

steps.text: Take the force's course on the new systems within six months
Keep working nights on the docks patrol
Keep saving 250 a month towards the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and it's the tech giants getting rich while working people scramble. I'd say it at the pub and at church. I'm not for the government running everything, but somebody has to slow this down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. The thinking parts of my job, the reports and the checks and maybe where we patrol, go in 2028. Then I'm basically the hands, and by 2031 a robot can be the hands. I'd be 31.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the woodwork seriously straight away. I'd start selling chopping boards and small furniture at the Saturday market, maybe 100 to 200 a month to start, and build it up. I'd cut back on the holidays and the takeaway nights. We'd pause the house hunt for a year until things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not wild, but I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why woodwork, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people pay for things made by a person, even when machines can do it. My grandad made furniture, and his chairs are still in my mum's kitchen. A handmade chair is the one thing a robot can't make handmade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Hanna's job carry you if yours went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. Care homes would still need people, at least till the robots, and probably after, because families want a person. But I'm not someone who'd want to be carried.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, with tech giants getting rich.
I'd say somebody has to **slow this down**, though I'm wary of big government.
think: The **thinking parts** of my job go in 2028.
By **2031** a robot could be the hands, and I'd be 31.
do: Sell **handmade boards** at the Saturday market, aiming for 100 to 200 a month.
Pause the **house hunt** for a year.
S2.quote: A handmade chair is the one thing a robot can't make handmade.
fieldNote: His fallback is a **family craft**, woodwork from his grandad.
He blames **tech giants** but stays wary of government doing too much.
He refuses to be **carried** by his partner, a matter of pride.

steps.text: Sell handmade chopping boards at the Saturday market
Pause the house hunt with Hanna for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the fast one, I'd say the tech giants are moving too quick. But with five years I'd also say people have time to sort themselves out. I'd say it to the lads on my shift who are panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build something on the side. I'd be 32 when the paperwork goes and about 35 when robots come for the patrol work. If the woodwork's paying properly by then, I'm not starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend about 1,500 on proper tools and turn half my dad's garage into a workshop in the first year. I'd ask a lad at church who does websites to help me sell online. I'd learn the AI tools at work once they're proven, because I'd need to use them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see it coming and I've got a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: 1,500 on tools is a chunk of your savings. Is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about a month of my savings, so yes, but it's a risk I can see. My dad says you don't regret buying good tools. And the deposit can wait a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave policing for the woodwork in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not before I have to. I'd want to do my full time on the docks as long as there's a job there. The workshop is for after, not instead.

say: I'd say the **tech giants** are moving too quick.
I'd tell **panicking** colleagues there's time to sort themselves out.
think: Five years is enough to **build something** on the side.
At **32 and 35** I wouldn't be starting from nothing.
do: Spend about **1,500 on tools** for a workshop in the garage.
Ask a church friend to help me **sell online**.
Learn AI tools at work once they're **proven**.
S3.quote: My dad says you don't regret buying good tools.
fieldNote: The extra time turns woodwork from **panic move** into a planned business.
He would stay in policing **as long as possible**.
He relies on **church and family** networks rather than courses.

steps.text: Spend about 1,500 on tools and set up a garage workshop
Get a church friend to build a website for his furniture
Learn the force's AI tools once colleagues have proven them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, people should stop panicking and start working on it. At church I'd probably say something about not putting our trust in machines. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be alright. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and nearly 40 when robots come. By then I'd hope to be married, with the house, a workshop going and maybe a sergeant's stripes. Hanna's job would still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd propose to Hanna, which I've been meaning to do anyway. We'd buy a house in the next two years, with a garage for the workshop. I'd keep the woodwork going at weekends and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The proposal is in this picture and not the fast one. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in the fast one I'd want to know where the money was coming from first. In this one there's time to do things in the right order. My dad always said: job, house, wedding, kids, in that order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids one day about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn a skill with their hands and to go to church, the same as my dad told me. I'd tell them machines come and go, but neighbours stay.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**; stop panicking and start working.
At church I'd talk about not putting **trust in machines**.
think: I'd be **alright**: married, a house, a workshop, maybe sergeant.
Hanna's **care home job** would still be there.
do: Buy a **house with a garage** in the next two years.
S4.quote: My dad always said: job, house, wedding, kids, in that order.
fieldNote: The long timeline **unlocks** his family plans: proposal and house.
His order of life comes straight from **his father**.
He leans on **faith** and neighbours more than policy for reassurance.

steps.text: Propose to Hanna in the first year
Keep making and selling furniture at weekends
Keep working docks nights and saving for a house with a garage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not enough time to build anything on the side, and the house would be off. What would help is the force being honest early about which jobs go when, and help for people starting small businesses, like cheaper workshop space or fewer forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the docks. The lads at the docks have been watching cranes get automated for years, and nobody listened to them. Ask them what it's like.

headlineQuote: The lads at the docks have been watching cranes get automated for years, and nobody listened to them.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old night officer** covering the docks and industrial estate, son of a firefighter.
He lives with Hanna, a **care home nurse**, and they are saving for a house.
He uses AI when it's **proven** and expects back-office staff to be hit first.
With fast AGI he turns his **woodwork** into a side business; with ten years he proposes.
His values are **work, faith** and family order: job, house, wedding, kids.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to build anything and putting the **house** off.
whatWouldHelp: The force being **honest early** about which jobs go when.
Help for **small businesses**, like cheaper workshop space and fewer forms.
